--- title: 'Sankey Diagrams and Network Graphs' author: 'Pinn Xu' date: '2024-12-05' # categories: ["Python", "Visualization", "Sankey Diagram", "Network Diagram", "Plotly"] categories: ["Python", "Plotly", "Sankey Diagram", "Network Diagram"] description: "Use Plotly, Pyvis & NetworkX to create sankey & network diagrams." order: 4 aliases: - ../sankey-and-network/ --- ::: {#ebe03135 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Environment and Versions"} python==3.12 pandas==2.2.2 plotly==5.24.1 matplotlib==3.9.x pyvis==0.3.2 networkx==3.3 ``` ::: # Sankey Diagrams ## What is a Sankey Diagram A **Sankey diagram** is a specific type of flow chart where branch widths are proportional to the flow quantity, used to visualize the transfer of energy, money, or materials. It is named after Matthew Henry Phineas Riall Sankey's 1898 diagram of steam engine energy efficiency [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankey_diagram). A Sankey diagram consists of **nodes** and **links**. Nodes represent stages or entities in a process; links represent the flow of resources between nodes, typically directed from a **source node** to a **target node**. The **width** of a link represents the flow quantity, and colors can distinguish different stages or categories. Flow is conserved: the sum of branch widths at each stage is equal. **Example 1:** The figure below (@fig-electricity-usage) shows the flow of electricity in a home: total power on the far left, rooms in the middle, and appliances on the right; link width represents flow quantity, and colors distinguish appliance types. ![Home electricity flow Sankey diagram](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig2-electricity-usage.png){#fig-electricity-usage} [(Image source: PPCexpo, Example #2)](https://ppcexpo.com/blog/energy-flow-diagram){.caption} **Example 2:** The figure below (@fig-store-orders) shows the classification of orders on a shopping website: starting from total orders, broken down by product category, subcategory, and brand; link width represents order quantity, and colors distinguish product categories. ![Shopping website order classification Sankey diagram](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig3-store-orders.png){#fig-store-orders} [(Image source: ChartExpo, Example #5)](https://chartexpo.com/blog/sankey-diagram-in-excel#){.caption} ## Plotly Graph Object We previously used `plotly.express` — Plotly's high-level interface for creating common charts with simple functions. Drawing Sankey diagrams requires the lower-level interface `plotly.graph_objects`. > **Low-Level Interface**: Provides basic functions that directly manipulate underlying data, requiring more code to write.\ > **High-Level Interface**: Provides highly integrated functions that are convenient to use but less flexible.\ > For example, `matplotlib.pyplot` is Matplotlib's high-level interface (`plt.hist()`), while importing the lower-level `matplotlib` module gives access to functions like `mpl.axes.Axes()`. ::: {#3cab1307 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Import plotly via low-level interface, aliased as go import plotly.graph_objects as go ``` ::: ## Functions and Classes We will use `go.Sankey()` to store Sankey diagram data, then use `go.Figure()` to render it. Strictly speaking, `go.Sankey()` is a **constructor** of a **class**, and calling it creates an object that stores the Sankey diagram data; the same applies to `go.Figure()`. Common Python terminology relationships are shown in @tbl-terminology: | Concept | Related Concept | Example | |:------:|:---------:|:------| | Function | Parameter | pd.read_csv(encoding='utf-8') | | Object | Method | `df.sample(size=10)` | | Class | Property | `go.Sankey(node=..., link=...)` | | Object | Attribute | `df.columns` | : Python terminology relationships (note: `pd`, `go` are library interfaces; `df` is a concrete object) {#tbl-terminology tbl-colwidths=[15,20,65]} ## Dictionaries A **dictionary (dict)** is a Python data structure that stores data as **key-value pairs**. There are three common ways to create one: ::: {#6d5787c9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Method 1 d1 = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3} # keys must be quoted # Method 2 d2 = dict(a=1, b=2, c=3) # no quotes needed # Method 3 keys = ['a', 'b', 'c'] # define keys and values separately values = [1, 2, 3] d3 = dict(zip(keys, values)) # zip() pairs them together, dict() converts to a dictionary print(d1) print(d2) print(d3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3} {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3} {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3} ``` ::: ::: **Key differences between lists and dictionaries:** - Lists are ordered, elements can repeat, and elements are accessed by position (index, starting from 0). - Dictionaries are unordered, keys must be unique (values can repeat), and values are accessed by key. ::: {#a740115c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Example: animals and their sounds animal_with_sound = {'cat': 'meow', 'dog': 'woof', 'duck': 'quack'} sound = ['meow', 'woof', 'quack'] ``` ::: ::: {#f72e8e7d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # List: access elements by position (index) sound[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 'meow' ``` ::: ::: ::: {#358ae925 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Dict: access values by key (note: dicts are unordered, cannot use index) animal_with_sound['cat'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 'meow' ``` ::: ::: ## Drawing Sankey Diagrams References: > [Plotly Official Sankey Diagram Tutorial](https://plotly.com/python/sankey-diagram/)\ > [plotly.graph_objects.Sankey() Documentation](https://plotly.com/python-api-reference/generated/plotly.graph_objects.Sankey.html) ### Building the Sankey Object **Step 1:** Use `go.Sankey()` to create the Sankey diagram object. In the node names, A/B/C represent three stages, and numbers represent different nodes within the same stage. ::: {#a4e95f0c .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Parameter configuration for go.Sankey() sankey_data = go.Sankey( # define the sankey_data variable ########################################################################## # Node node = dict( # Node labels label = ['A1','A2','B1','B2','C1','C2'], # Node colors: one-to-one correspondence with node labels color = [ 'yellow', 'yellow', 'tomato', 'tomato', 'cornflowerblue', 'cornflowerblue', ], # Node spacing (padding) and thickness (unit: px) pad = 30, thickness = 20, # Node border line = dict( color = 'black', # border color width = 5, # border width (unit: px) ) ), ########################################################################## # Link link = dict( # Source nodes: index in the node label list source = [0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 3], # Target nodes: index in the node label list target = [2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5], # Link flow values: corresponding to source and target lists value = [8, 4, 2, 8, 4, 2], # Link colors: corresponding to the above color = [ 'sandybrown', 'sandybrown', 'sandybrown', 'thistle', 'thistle', 'thistle', ], # Link arrow length: pointing from source to target (default 0, no arrow) arrowlen = 15 ) ) ############################################################################## # Check the data type of sankey_data print('Data type:\n', type(sankey_data),'\n') # Check the content of sankey_data print('Content:\n', sankey_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Data type: Content: Sankey({ 'link': {'arrowlen': 15, 'color': [sandybrown, sandybrown, sandybrown, thistle, thistle, thistle], 'source': [0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 3], 'target': [2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5], 'value': [8, 4, 2, 8, 4, 2]}, 'node': {'color': [yellow, yellow, tomato, tomato, cornflowerblue, cornflowerblue], 'label': [A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2], 'line': {'color': 'black', 'width': 5}, 'pad': 30, 'thickness': 20} }) ``` ::: ::: As seen from the output, `sankey_data` is a Plotly Sankey object, with parameters stored in nested dictionaries. When building a Sankey object, note that values in the source and target node lists are **indices** into the node label list, not node names themselves. For example, `0` in `source = [0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 3]` refers to the first node 'A1', `1` refers to the second node 'A2', and so on. Therefore, you must ensure that indices match the order of nodes in the label list, otherwise links will point to the wrong nodes. ### Rendering the Figure **Step 2:** Use `go.Figure()` to render the figure: ::: {#cell-fig-sankey-sample .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Render figure fig = go.Figure(sankey_data) # Update layout fig.update_layout( height=400, title_text='Sample Sankey Diagram', title_x=0.5, title_y=0.95, # title position margin=dict( l=60, r=60, t=60, b=20, ), font={'style': 'italic'}, ) # Display figure # fig.show(renderer='notebook') # if use VS Code or Jupyter, use this line fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-sankey-sample .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Sample Sankey Diagram ::: ::: As shown in @fig-sankey-sample, A/B/C represent three stages, and numbers represent different nodes within the same stage. Link width represents flow quantity, and colors distinguish different stages or categories. ### Pre-defining Variables As the number of nodes grows, managing indices becomes difficult. To address this, we can define a dictionary to **look up the index of a node by its name**, making the data construction more intuitive: ::: {#2d3ff151 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Define a list variable to store node names node_names = ['A1', 'A2', 'B1', 'B2', 'C1', 'C2'] # Generate index list corresponding to nodes using range(len()) node_ids = range(len(node_names)) # Build a name-to-index dictionary nodes = dict(zip(node_names, node_ids)) ``` ::: ::: {#08ff121d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} nodes['B2'] # look up the index for a node by name ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: This allows you to look up the index of **source nodes** and **target nodes** in the **node label list** by name. At the same time, for long parameters, you can **pre-define variables and pass them into the function**, making the code cleaner and easier to maintain. The following code redraws the same Sankey diagram shown in @fig-sankey-sample above: ::: {#cell-fig-sankey-sample-new .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ############################################################################## # Values needed for node parameters # Define node colors node_colors = [ 'yellow', 'yellow', 'tomato', 'tomato', 'cornflowerblue', 'cornflowerblue', ] # Define the complete node parameter node_definition = dict( pad=15, thickness=20, line=dict(color='black', width=5), label=node_names, # use the node name variable defined above color=node_colors, # use the node color variable just defined ) ############################################################################## # Values needed for link parameters # Look up indices by node name to define sources and targets sources = [ nodes['A1'], nodes['A1'], nodes['A2'], nodes['B1'], nodes['B2'], nodes['B2'], ] targets = [ nodes['B1'], nodes['B2'], nodes['B2'], nodes['C1'], nodes['C1'], nodes['C2'], ] # Define link flow values and colors values = [8, 4, 2, 8, 4, 2] link_colors = [ 'sandybrown', 'sandybrown', 'sandybrown', 'thistle', 'thistle', 'thistle', ] # Define the complete link parameter link_definition = dict( source=sources, target=targets, value=values, color=link_colors, arrowlen=15, ) ############################################################################## # Draw the Sankey diagram # Pass the pre-defined node_definition and link_definition into the function fig = go.Figure( go.Sankey( node = node_definition, link = link_definition, ) ) # Update layout fig.update_layout( height=400, title_text='Sample Sankey Diagram - Redrawn', title_x=0.5, title_y=0.95, margin=dict( l=60, r=60, t=60, b=20, ), font={'style': 'italic'}, ) fig.show() # display the chart ``` ::: {#fig-sankey-sample-new .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Sample Sankey Diagram - Redrawn ::: ::: The redrawn result is identical to the original. But by pre-defining data as variables, you only need to adjust variable values when modifying data, making the code cleaner and easier to maintain. ### Modifying Color Transparency To **modify link color transparency**, use RGBA values instead of color name strings. The RGBA format is `(red, green, blue, alpha)`, where `alpha` represents opacity (0 = fully transparent, 1 = fully opaque). Both `"sandybrown"` and `"thistle"` are CSS preset color names, which can be found at [w3schools CSS Colors](https://www.w3schools.com/cssref/css_colors.php) or the [Matplotlib Color Reference](https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/color/named_colors.html). ::: {#d354f635 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Import library for handling RGBA values import matplotlib.colors as c ``` ::: ::: {#55095c38 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Use c.to_rgba() to find RGB values and set alpha c.to_rgba('sandybrown', 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` (0.9568627450980393, 0.6431372549019608, 0.3764705882352941, 0.5) ``` ::: ::: Plotly supports specifying RGBA colors using the string format `'rgba(r, g, b, a)'`. ::: {#27298d02 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Define strings to store RGBA values for transparent colors faint_sandybrown = 'rgba' + str(c.to_rgba('sandybrown', 0.5)) # + concatenates strings faint_thistle = 'rgba' + str(c.to_rgba('thistle', 0.5)) # Print the strings print(faint_sandybrown) print(faint_thistle) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rgba(0.9568627450980393, 0.6431372549019608, 0.3764705882352941, 0.5) rgba(0.8470588235294118, 0.7490196078431373, 0.8470588235294118, 0.5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-sankey-sample-faint .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Redefine link colors link_colors = [ faint_sandybrown, faint_sandybrown, faint_sandybrown, faint_thistle, faint_thistle, faint_thistle, ] # Update chart fig.update_traces(link_color=link_colors) fig.update_layout( height=400, title_text='Sample Sankey Diagram - 50% Link Transparency', title_x=0.5, title_y=0.95, margin=dict( l=60, r=60, t=60, b=20, ), font={'style': 'italic'}, ) fig.show() ``` ::: {#fig-sankey-sample-faint .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Sample Sankey Diagram - 50% Link Transparency ::: ::: # Network Graphs ## Comparing Sankey Diagrams and Network Graphs Both Sankey diagrams and network graphs visualize relational data, but with different emphases, as shown in @tbl-sankey-vs-network: | Feature | Sankey Diagram | Network Graph | |:-------:|:---------------:|:-------------:| | Primary Use | Visualize resource flow quantities | Visualize connections between nodes | | Node Meaning | Process stage or entity | Individual (e.g., a user) | | Connection Name | Link | Edge | | Connection Direction | Directed (source → target) | Can be directed or undirected | | Connection Width | Represents flow quantity | No width distinction | | Key Characteristics | Hierarchical, flow conservation | Connection strength and relational distance | | Application Examples | Energy distribution, cost allocation | Social networks, computer networks | : Comparison of Sankey Diagrams and Network Graphs {#tbl-sankey-vs-network tbl-colwidths=[20,35,45]} ## Drawing Network Graphs Install `pyvis` before use (includes networkx). ::: {#003b0011 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} pip install pyvis ``` ::: In a local environment (Jupyter), installation persists and can be reused; in Google Colab's virtual environment, installation only applies to the current file and must be repeated for new files. ::: {#94a52e7e .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Import libraries for drawing network graphs from pyvis.network import Network import networkx as nx ``` ::: **Step 1: Create network relationships with networkx** ::: {#666effac .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create an empty undirected graph gx = nx.Graph() # Note: use nx.MultiDiGraph() to create a directed graph instead ``` ::: ::: {#85fb5a51 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Add nodes and edges to the empty graph gx gx.add_edge('a', 'b') # edge from 'a' to 'b' gx.add_edge('b', 'd') gx.add_edge('c', 'e') gx.add_edge('e', 'a') gx.add_edge('c', 'd') ``` ::: **Step 2: Output an interactive network graph with pyvis** ::: {#4c01f348 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create an empty interactive network graph object gp = Network() # Load network relationships from gx gp.from_nx(gx) # Output as a standalone HTML file gp.show('net.html', notebook=False) # notebook=False let the fig not be rendered in Jupyter output cell # only use True when you are using Jupyter & browser ``` ::: The output standalone HTML file is saved in the current directory ([view source code and files](https://github.com/Pinn32/pinn32.github.io/tree/main/zh/tutorials/sankey-and-network)). In Colab, it can be found in the left file panel, as shown in @fig-colab. Download it and open it in a browser to see the result shown in @fig-network-sample. ![The output HTML file is automatically saved in Colab's file panel](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig6-colab.png){#fig-colab} ![Network graph HTML output demonstration (animated GIF)](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig7-network-sample.gif){#fig-network-sample width="60%"} ::: {#85de4db7 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(gp.nodes[0]) # view info for the first node (index 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` {'color': '#97c2fc', 'size': 10, 'id': 'a', 'label': 'a', 'shape': 'dot'} ``` ::: ::: **Manually modifying node attributes:** ::: {#729800cf .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Modify node attributes gp.nodes[0]['color'] = 'red' # color gp.nodes[0]['size'] = 20 # size # Rename the output file to avoid overwriting the original gp.show('net-modified.html', notebook=False) ``` ::: The modified result is shown in @fig-network-sample-modified: ![Modified network graph](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig8-network-sample-modified.png){#fig-network-sample-modified width="50%"} ## Displaying Network in Output Cells There are a few approaches to render interactive network diagrams in output cells (see [this blog](/en/blogs/2025-10-07-fix-network-diagram/)). Below shows the approach with the most adaptability that can render networks in any environment without external files or dependencies. ::: {#dee47d97 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from IPython.display import HTML, display # store network's html code html = gp.generate_html() # format: only use double quotes html_formatted = html.replace("'",'"') # defining iframe tag iframe_start = """ " # wrap formatted html code with iframe tag html_wrapped = iframe_start + html_formatted + iframe_end # display display(HTML(html_wrapped)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Reading Network Relationships from a File In addition to manual creation, network relationship data can also be read from a CSV file. The following example uses ***beer and curry*** tweet data [(view source file)](https://github.com/Pinn32/pinn32.github.io/blob/main/src/data/beer-and-curry.csv): original posters mentioned other users, forming directed edges from the original poster (source node) to the mentioned user (target node). ::: {#03bdbf0a .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} ############################################################################### # Data preprocessing # Import pandas to handle the CSV file import pandas as pd # Read the CSV file path = '../../../src/data/beer-and-curry.csv' df = pd.read_csv(path) # Drop rows with no mentions df.dropna(subset='mentions', inplace=True) ############################################################################### # Create network relationships # Create an empty directed graph gx1 = nx.MultiDiGraph() # Loop over all rows for i in df.index: user = df.loc[i, 'user'] # get the user as source node mentions = df.loc[i, 'mentions'] # get all mentions in a post mentions = mentions.replace(' ', '') # remove spaces mentions = mentions.split('@') # split by '@' to get individual mentions mentions.pop(0) # first element after split is empty, remove it for mention in mentions: gx1.add_edge(user, mention) # add all nodes and edges ############################################################################### # Draw the network graph gp1 = Network() # create an empty network graph gp1.from_nx(gx1) # load network relationships gp1.show('net-from-csv.html', notebook=False) # output HTML file ``` ::: The output network graph is complex; rendering may take 1–2 minutes — do not close the browser during this time. The overall view is shown in @fig-network-overview, and a detail view in @fig-network-detail. ![Social network graph: overall view](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig9-network-overview.png){#fig-network-overview} ![Social network graph: detail view](../../../src/img/ttl/sankey/fig10-network-detail.png){#fig-network-detail} Network graphs can be used to study social networks, identify strong/weak connections and high-influence users, and analyze potential information cocoon or echo chamber phenomena.
